newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia, Libya award oil block to Saudi/Malay group.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia, Libya award oil block to Saudi/Malay group.

text.p: Tunisia and Libya have awarded a Saudi-Malyasian consortium a contract to explore a shared offshore oil field in the Gulf of Gabes, energy officials said on Tuesday.

They said Joint Oil, a venture between the Libyan and Tunisian state-run oil companies, signed with Saudi private firm Nimir Petroleum Company Ltd and Malaysia's state oil firm Petronas an exploration and production sharing agreement covering the offshore block "7th November".
Joint Oil chairman Tarek Bek told Reuters in an interview that the consortium will spend at least $30 million during the first exploration period of five years, plus a possible one year extension.

He said the figure includes the drilling of three firm and one conditionnal exploration wells by the second half of 1998, seismic acquisition covering 2,600 km square of 2D and 300 km square of 3D, and the reprocessing of 1,800 km of pre-existing seismic data. The contract has a total duration of 30 years.
The "7th November" block has a minimum 260 to 300 million barrels recoverable reserves in its main structure, Bek said.
The block covers 3,000 kilometres square, half in Tunisia, half in Libya.

The deal was signed last February and ratified on Monday at Joint Oil's headquarters in the Tunisian island of Djerba by Tunisian Industry Minister Slaheddine Bouguerra and Libyan Energy Minister Abdullah Salem al-Badri.

The consortium is formed by Nimir Petroleum Company North Africa (NPC/NA), operator with 55 percent, and Petronas Carigali Overseas Sdn Bhd (PCOSB) with 45 percent, respectively fully owned by Nimir Petroleum and Petronas.
"The consortium would assume all the spending," Bek said.
He said that Joint Oil would get 35/39 percent of the profit.
The governments of Libya and Tunisia in 1989 established Joint Oil to jointly exploit the concession.

Joint Oil has already invested in seismic surveys by French company Compagnie Generale de Geophysique, but in 1992 it decided to invite foreign oil companies to finance the exploration work, instead of undertaking the drillings of its own.
The concession area is about 150 km (93 miles) north of the Libyan coast and 120 km (76 miles) to the north-east of the island of Djerba. The water depth averages 100 metres.
The two countries decided to jointly exploit it, ending a long dispute over ownership.

"It is promising because it is surrounded by the Libyan offshore field of Bouri, which is 30 km (19 miles) south, the field of Isis which is three km (two miles) north, and the (British Gas') gas field of Miskar which is seven km (four miles) west," Bek said.
The Libyan Bouri block is the greatest offshore field in the Mediterranean.
Last year, Tunisia and Libya agreed to guarantee the freedom of movement for workers involved in the exploration and production, and tax exemption for equipment used.
